extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agencies, administrative-law practitioners, policy makers, and members of the public who draft or evaluate notice-and-comment submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and producing public comments for administrative notice-and-comment rulemaking in the era of AI (including use or misuse of models like ChatGPT). Emphasis on criteria that distinguish high-value, verifiable comments from low-quality AI-generated mass submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of identity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should favor comments that include verifiable identifying information. Authentication and identity verification are a central challenge in the AI era; low-quality or AI-generated mass comments typically do not include verifiable personal identifiers. Guidance: include names, contact information, institutional affiliation, or other verifiable data as appropriate to show the commenter is who they claim to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive originality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments should contribute content that is new to the agency rather than simply repeating the agency's own language. Low-quality AI-generated comments often use generic templates or surface variation and may simply repeat agency text back without analysis. Agencies should prioritize original arguments, novel evidence, or unique perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific factual content that AI cannot fabricate
rubrics_metrics.description: include specific facts only known to the commenter (that AI cannot fabricate reliably)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that contain verifiable, specific factual details — e.g., dates, locations, personal experiences, primary-documents reviewed, or proprietary data — are harder for AI to fabricate and therefore more persuasive. Low-quality comments lack these specifics. Advice for commenters: provide facts that can be checked (and cite sources) to establish credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with specific provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: engage with specific provisions, sections, or pages of the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality comments engage section-by-section with the proposed regulatory text, including specific citations to sections or page numbers and tailored analysis of how a proposal would operate in practice. Low-quality AI comments tend not to engage with specific section/page citations or the details of particular provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal expertise/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: personal expertise or experience that grounds the comment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments grounded in the commenter's personal expertise, professional role, or lived experience carry more weight. Provide identifiable expertise or institutional affiliation and explain how that experience informs the comment. Absence of such grounding is a common feature of low-quality AI-generated submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal stories with verifiable specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: use of personal stories that include verifiable specifics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper explicitly recommends personal stories with verifiable specifics as effective content: these stories should include checkable details (dates, locations, documents) to make them persuasive and resistant to fabrication. Such stories help agencies assess real-world impacts and claimant credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations to documents the commenter has personally reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: cite documents the commenter has personally reviewed to support assertions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing and referencing documents the commenter has actually reviewed (and can identify precisely) strengthens a submission's credibility. These citations serve as verifiable anchors for claims and are preferable to generic, uncited assertions. Where possible, include exact document titles, authors, dates, and page references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original data or analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: provide original data or analysis rather than only summary or opinion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting original datasets, empirical analysis, calculations, or other novel evidence increases substantive value. Agencies should treat original analysis as higher-quality than restated summaries. The paper highlights original data/analysis as a way for commenters to add value in an AI-saturated comment environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific section-by-section engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: structured, section-by-section critique or support of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond merely citing provisions, commenters should provide structured comments that walk through the proposal section-by-section, explaining consequences, proposing alternative language, or identifying implementation concerns. This is emphasized in the paper as necessary to distinguish detailed, useful comments from generic mass submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifiable expertise or institutional affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: clear statement of the commenter's qualifications or institutional role
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state any institutional affiliation, professional credentials, or roles that give the commenter standing or subject-matter credibility. The paper treats identifiable expertise or affiliation as key to grounding comments and to enabling agencies to weigh competing inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of AI assistance (open question)
rubrics_metrics.description: whether and how commenters should disclose use of AI in drafting comments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper raises, but does not resolve, the question of what disclosure should be required when AI generates substantial portions of a comment. Agencies may need rules or guidance on disclosure of AI assistance; until then, commenters should consider voluntarily disclosing AI use and clarifying which portions are human-authored versus AI-assisted.
